title: Psalm 54: Save Me by Your Name
summary: Betrayed by people who should have protected him, David asks God to save and vindicate him by his name and might. Ruthless men seek his life without regard for God, but David declares that God is his helper and the sustainer of his life. He promises a freewill offering and thanks God for delivering him from every trouble.
story: Psalm 54 is one of the shortest laments in the Psalter, and one of several psalms tied to David's years as a fugitive from Saul. It follows the portrait of universal corruption in Psalm 53 with one man's plea in a specific crisis. Its movement, from urgent plea to confident thanksgiving in seven verses, is the pattern of many laments: the situation has not changed, but the one praying has placed it in God's hands. It stands next to Psalm 55, where betrayal by a close friend is the theme.
historical:
The heading ties the psalm to the time when the Ziphites went to Saul and said, "Is David not hiding among us?" The story is told in 1 Samuel 23:19-29, with a similar episode in 1 Samuel 26:1. Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah, southeast of Hebron, near the wilderness where David and his men were hiding. The Ziphites, fellow Judeans, went to Saul at Gibeah and offered to hand David over. Saul pursued David and nearly caught him at a place called the Rock of Escape, but withdrew when word came that the Philistines were raiding the land (1 Samuel 23:27-28). If the heading is followed, the psalm belongs to the late eleventh century BC.

As with other historical headings, many scholars regard this one as an editorial link rather than part of the original poem. The psalm itself speaks of "strangers" rising against the psalmist, a word some find odd for fellow Judeans, though it can mean people who acted as outsiders or foreigners to the faith. Psalm 86:14 contains a nearly identical line using a word for "arrogant" instead, which may explain the difference.
cultural:
In the ancient world, a person's name expressed their character and identity. God's name, revealed to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14-15), represented who he is and what he has promised to do. To be saved "by Your name" is to appeal to God's revealed character, as opposed to magical use of divine names, which was common in the surrounding cultures.

The freewill offering of verse 6 (nedavah) was a voluntary sacrifice, not required by law or vow, offered purely out of gratitude (Leviticus 7:16; 22:18-23). It expressed a worshiper's thankfulness beyond obligation. The phrase "my eyes have stared down my foes" (verse 7) reflects the language of victory: to look upon one's enemies in triumph, having seen them defeated or withdrawn.
literary: The psalm has a simple two-part structure, divided by "Selah" after verse 3. Verses 1 to 3 are the plea: save me, vindicate me, hear me, because enemies seek my life. Verses 4 to 7 are the confidence and vow: God is my helper, he will repay my enemies, I will sacrifice and praise. God's name frames the psalm, appearing in verse 1 ("Save me, O God, by Your name") and verse 6 ("I will praise Your name, O LORD, for it is good"). The shift from "God" to "LORD" in verse 6 is notable in the Elohistic Psalter, where the personal name is used sparingly.

doctrines.note: God's name stands for his character and his promises. The psalmist appeals not to his own strength but to who God has shown himself to be.
The psalm moves from urgent request to settled thanksgiving without the situation visibly changing. Prayer here reorders the one who prays around God's faithfulness.
In the story behind the heading, Saul's pursuit is broken off by a Philistine raid. The psalm reads such turns not as chance but as God delivering "from every trouble".

words.note: Shem, name. God's name is his revealed identity and reputation. It frames the psalm: David asks to be saved by God's name and ends by praising it, because it is good.

Azar, to help. "Surely God is my helper" (verse 4) is the psalm's central confession. The related noun ezer describes God as Israel's help and is also used of the woman in Genesis 2:18, where it implies strength, not inferiority.
Nedavah, freewill offering or voluntariness. BSB translates it "Freely" in verse 6. It was a gift beyond duty, offered simply out of gratitude, the natural response of someone who has been rescued.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 54, and the connection is thematic. Like David, Jesus was betrayed by those who should have welcomed him and handed over to the authorities by one of his own people. The psalm's appeal to God's name is taken up in the New Testament, where salvation is found in the name of Jesus (Acts 4:12) and God gives him the name above every name (Philippians 2:9-11). The freewill offering of thanks also anticipates Christian worship, which is offered not to earn God's favor but in grateful response to a deliverance already given.

hard.q: How can the psalmist pray, "In Your faithfulness, destroy them"?
hard.a: This is a prayer for God's justice against people seeking an innocent man's life. It asks God to act, rather than taking revenge personally, and it appeals to God's faithfulness to his promises to protect the righteous. In the story behind the heading, David repeatedly refused to harm Saul himself (1 Samuel 24 and 26), leaving judgment to God. Christians read such prayers in light of Jesus' command to love enemies and pray for persecutors (Matthew 5:44). Some see these psalms as honest cries that trust God with justice; others see them as expressing a stage of revelation the New Testament goes beyond. Most agree that handing vengeance to God is itself an act of restraint.

questions: What does it mean to ask God to save you "by Your name"? What in God's character do you appeal to when you pray?
The Ziphites were David's own countrymen. How do you respond when people who should support you turn against you?
The freewill offering was given beyond what was required. What would a freewill offering of gratitude look like in your life?
